Receipt
re-seet'
n. (the place of receiving; in all three Gospels, the tax booth from which Matthew rose and followed Christ)
From Latin recepta, things received, through Old French recete — the p was inserted later in imitation of the Latin and was never sounded. The Greek phrase is telonion, the tax-office or toll booth, from telos, a tax.

Biblical Definition

The word occurs three times and always in the same phrase, the receipt of custom — the booth where tolls were collected on goods passing through. Matthew records his own call in the third person: “as Jesus passed forth from thence, he saw a man, named Matthew, sitting at the receipt of custom: and he saith unto him, Follow me. And he arose, and followed him” (Matthew 9:9). Mark and Luke give the man his other name: “he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the receipt of custom” (Mark 2:14); “saw a publican, named Levi, sitting at the receipt of custom” (Luke 5:27). Luke adds the detail that makes the call cost something: “And he left all, rose up, and followed him” (Luke 5:28). The fishermen could return to their nets and did, after the crucifixion; a tax farmer who walked away from his booth could never have it back, since the franchise would be sold to another man that week. Of all the disciples, Matthew burned the most decisively. He then made Christ a great feast in his own house and filled it with publicans, which is the first thing he did with what he had left.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines receipt as the act of receiving, the place of receiving, and a written acknowledgment of something received — citing the receipt of custom.

expand to see more

RECEIPT, n. The act of receiving; as, the receipt of a letter.

2. The place of receiving; as the receipt of custom. Matt. 9.

3. A writing acknowledging the taking of money or goods.

4. Reception; admission.

CUSTOM, n. Tribute, toll or tax paid to the sovereign on goods imported or exported.

Key Scripture

Matthew 9:9 — "And as Jesus passed forth from thence, he saw a man, named Matthew, sitting at the receipt of custom: and he saith unto him, Follow me. And he arose, and followed him."

Mark 2:14 — "And as he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the receipt of custom, and said unto him, Follow me. And he arose and followed him."

Luke 5:27 — "And after these things he went forth, and saw a publican, named Levi, sitting at the receipt of custom: and he said unto him, Follow me."

Luke 5:28 — "And he left all, rose up, and followed him."

Modern Corruption

The call is softened into an invitation Matthew considered, when all three Gospels record a command obeyed on the spot at unrecoverable cost.

expand to see more

Modern presentations of conversion make the sinner the deciding party: Christ offers, the man weighs it, and at length he accepts. The three accounts of Matthew's call read otherwise. Christ passes by, sees the man, says two words, and the man rises. There is no recorded deliberation, no interval, and nothing in the text about Matthew's prior interest. What is described is an effectual call — a summons that carries its own power to be obeyed — and it is the ordinary New Testament pattern, from Lazarus at the tomb to Saul on the road. Reformed theology did not invent that doctrine; it read it out of scenes like this one.

The cost is easy to miss and Luke will not let it be missed: he left all. A tax booth was a purchased franchise on a trade route, and a man who walked away from it at midday had no way back. Matthew is also the disciple who, having lost his income, gave a great feast — and filled the guest list with the only society he had, publicans and sinners, so that the Pharisees complained and our Lord answered that the whole need no physician. The first act of the man who left all was to spend what remained on getting his old associates into a room with Christ.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek telonion, the tax booth — Matthew 9:9, Mark 2:14, Luke 5:27; telones, a publican; akoloutheo, to follow — the verb of the response.

expand to see more

Greek telonion — the toll-house or tax booth; the phrase “the receipt of custom” in all three Gospels.

Greek telones — a tax collector, publican; Luke 5:27 of Levi.

Greek akoloutheo — to follow, accompany as a disciple; the verb in every account.

Greek anistemi — to rise up; “he arose, and followed him.”

Latin recepta, things received — the source of the English word; the p was never sounded.

Usage

"“Sitting at the receipt of custom” — the tax booth on the trade route."

"“He arose, and followed him” — no recorded deliberation, and no way back."

"“He left all” — and then spent what remained on a feast for publicans."
